prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active peptide form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for B016 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. All six members independently chose B016 as the only preferred part, but I rest the case on the science. Proglucagon processing, the identification of the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) peptide and its action in humans are original, were confirmed by many groups over decades, and visibly changed how a whole field understands gut-pancreas signalling. The consequences, in glycaemic control, weight, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes, are documented in large randomized trials, so maturity is not in doubt. Holst, Drucker and Mojsov each hold a distinct step in the chain: human physiology of secretion and action, proglucagon-derived peptide biology and the receptor, and identification of the bioactive peptide. Consistent with the view that the prize recognises a specific discovery and not a career or a product, the citation is built around physiology and the active peptide, with the therapy as its consequence.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary remains the weakness, and round 1 did not remove it. Habener lies outside the supplied credit list and may hold a real priority claim on the active peptide; I cannot settle that from the files I may use, and I should not pretend otherwise. Excluding Knudsen means the prize may be read as ignoring the long-acting analogue that made the medicine practical, and the line I draw between discovery and development is a judgment, not a fact. Mojsov's contribution is also less prominent in the literature than Holst's or Drucker's. A single-part prize on a candidate that everyone ranks first carries the risk of consensus by default, which is a fair point from Wahren-Herlenius. If the committee cannot agree on a defensible three names, the unfolded protein response is the cleaner credit story and I would want it considered.

responses.point: Names Holst, Drucker and Knudsen, with a citation that explicitly includes the development of long-acting GLP-1 therapies, and keeps the unfolded protein response as the scientifically cleanest discovery.
responses.response: I have taken the Knudsen argument seriously, and I accept that the acylated analogue is what turned the biology into a medicine. My difficulty is the principle. If the prize explicitly honours development of long-acting therapies, we reward a drug program inside a prize for discovery, and the same logic would pull other industrial contributors into the credit and make the three-name limit harder to hold. Mojsov's identification of the active peptide is a discovery step on which the analogue work depended, so I keep her and word the citation around physiology and the active peptide, leaving the drug class as consequence. I agree with you that the unfolded protein response is the cleanest mechanistic story, and it remains my first alternative, but I do not think contested credit in GLP-1 is a reason to rank it lower in impact.

responses.point: Names Drucker, Holst and Mojsov in the final round-1 configuration, but his statement worries that the prize drifts toward industrial development and that the clinical story overshadows the physiological discovery. He lists B010 and CAR-T as alternatives.
responses.response: Your configuration is the same as mine, so the chair's question about whether you moved from Knudsen to Mojsov appears settled by your own file, and I read it as five of six for the trio. I share your concern about the clinical story overshadowing the physiology, and I think it is the best argument for the citation wording I propose: it names the physiology and the active peptide and does not name the drugs. On CAR-T as your second alternative, I remain hesitant while the credit list lacks the originators of the chimeric receptor concept, such as Eshhar, so I keep B010 and B044 as my alternatives instead, and I would accept B010 as the stronger fallback if the GLP-1 allocation stalls.

responses.point: Asks that the scientific case for GLP-1 be tested and not assumed, and warns that a single-part prize on a universally top-ranked candidate could be consensus by default. She moved from Knudsen to Mojsov on the principle that the prize is for discovery.
responses.response: I think the test is worth doing, and my answer is that the case survives it on its own evidence. Originality, independent replication, and lasting change in the field are met by the proglucagon and active peptide work, whatever the ranking counts. Your move to Mojsov rests on the same discovery-versus-development principle I use, which is helpful because it gives the committee a rule that can be applied beyond this ballot. I also agree that a second part would add attribution burdens, which you note for TOR and CAR-T. I would add a second part only if it were scientifically as strong as GLP-1 and had a clean credit, and nothing on the shortlist meets both conditions.

responses.point: Raises as chair the question of whether the prize should be single-part or two-part, notes that long-term safety of chronic incretin therapy is still accumulating, and offers optogenetics and the unfolded protein response as alternatives.
responses.response: On the single-part question I stay with one part. The unfolded protein response is a strong two-person discovery, but adding it would not fix the weakness in GLP-1, which is the third name, and it would make a prize with a very different centre of gravity. Optogenetics adds the problem we both noted, six credited names for three places, with Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck excluded under any trio. On long-term safety I take your point, but the prize is for the discovery of the physiology and the active peptide, which does not depend on how chronic therapy performs over decades, so I do not treat it as a reason to wait. I would be open to B010 as a second part only if the committee fails to agree on three GLP-1 names.

uncertainties: Priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, including Habener's contribution, cannot be verified from the files I may use and could change both the three names and the citation wording.
Whether the discovery-versus-development line, which I use to prefer Mojsov over Knudsen, will be accepted by a majority, since sandberg-rickard holds the other view.
Whether the optogenetics credit (B044) can be reduced to three people without an unjustifiable exclusion.
Whether the committee will want a second part, and if so whether the credit for it can be made as clean as the unfolded protein response.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on the shortlist. I disclose, as before, my earlier Salk collaboration with Ronald Evans, who is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I also note, as other members did in round 1, about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson, who chairs, and a 2009 co-authored paper with Abdel El Manira. Neither concerns a shortlisted discovery, and I request no recusal. I do not treat shared institutional affiliation or research topic as a conflict.
